# Naming & Ubiquitous Language

*LLM first draft · human-edited once · LLM novice pass · human-reviewed*

## The same thing, called three things

A lending codebase has a class called `Record`, a database row the team calls an
`Entry`, and a `LoanDto` that crosses one boundary. All three are the same
idea: a loan. Nobody wrote that down. Every reader works it out again, and
holds a little translation table in their head while they read.

Nothing is broken. No test fails. It costs a few minutes per reader, forever,
and it makes search unreliable: looking for "loan" finds a third of the places
loans are handled.

This Module is about paying that cost once instead of on every reading.

## The cheapest change with the highest leverage

Renaming is the cheapest change you can make to a codebase. No behavior moves.
When the tests sit at the Target Interface — the fixed outer edge of the code,
which names on the inside cannot affect — nothing breaks.

It is also the highest-leverage change, because a name is read hundreds of
times for every once it is written: by you, by the next reader, and by every AI
tool you work with. A model prompted in the domain's own words writes code you
do not have to translate back. A model prompted over `Manager`s and
`ProcessData`s guesses.

## One concept, one name — everywhere

A **domain** is the subject your program is about: lending, ticketing, payroll.
A **Ubiquitous Language** is one agreed list of words for the things in that
domain, used everywhere — in conversation, in documents, in commit messages,
and in code.

The rule has two halves. One concept gets exactly one name. One name means
exactly one concept. When the domain says *loan*, the code says `Loan` — not
`Record` in one file and `Entry` in another. When a concept has no name yet,
name it first, then write the code.

The payoff is mechanical, not a matter of taste.

- Search for a domain word and you find every place the code touches that
  concept. Grep becomes a design tool.
- A sentence spoken by someone who knows the business turns into code almost
  word for word, and back again.
- A new reader predicts what a method does from its signature alone, before
  opening the body.

## Four checks that need no taste

A good name states what the reader would otherwise have to discover by reading
the implementation. A bad name forces that reading — or lies, so the reader
trusts it and is wrong. Four ways to tell them apart with nobody's opinion
involved:

1. **The prediction check.** Read only the name and the signature, and write
   down what you expect the member to do. Then read the body. Anything the body
   did that your prediction missed — or promised and skipped — is a naming
   defect, whichever direction it runs.
2. **The synonym count.** Pick one domain concept and search for every word the
   code uses for it. A count above one means every reader carries the
   translation table from the top of this page.
3. **The vague-word grep.** Search for `Manager`, `Helper`, `Util`, `Handler`,
   `Process`, `Data`, `Info`, `temp`, `flag`, and `item`. Each hit announces
   *that a thing exists* without saying what it is or does. Ask of each one:
   which noun or verb from this member's one-sentence job is missing from its
   name?
4. **The scope-honesty check.** A **side effect** is anything a call changes
   besides producing its answer. Count the side effects the name does not
   mention — a `Get` that creates a row, a `Validate` that saves. Any count
   above zero is a lie the codebase tells hundreds of times.

## A name that will not come is a design probe

Naming is not decoration applied after the design. It is the cheapest design
review you can run.

When a class cannot be named without *and*, *or*, or a vague word, it usually
holds more than one responsibility, and the missing name is telling you where to
split it. State each class's responsibility in one sentence beginning with its
name: a sentence that needs "and" was two classes.

When two parts of a system use different words for the same concept, the line
between them forces every caller to translate. That line is a **seam** — a
place where a system naturally comes apart, and so a place where a boundary can
be drawn cleanly. A clash of vocabulary marks a seam that needs one owner and
one word.

## How this runs in your Exercises

- In the refactor-type Exercise the behavior is already correct and the Test
  Suite starts green. The flaw planted for you to find — the **Smell** — is
  entirely in the names. The Target Interface's names are the Ubiquitous
  Language; rename everything behind it into that language, keeping the suite
  green after each step.
- In the construct-type Exercise the temptation is to let implementation
  vocabulary write the code: `dict`, `entry`, `flag`, a helper called
  `Manager`. The folder's glossary is the domain's language, and every name you
  introduce comes from it.
- Either way, finish with the four checks above. The Self-Check asks the same
  countable questions, and they are the questions to ask of every piece of code
  you and an AI write together from now on.

modelExamples.caption: A pure rename — identical behavior, line for line — moved the class from borrowed vocabulary (Manager, Process, Item, Data, temp) into the clinic's Ubiquitous Language. Before: grep for the domain words finds nothing, and every reader re-derives what ProcessItem means. After: the code and the domain expert's sentence are the same sentence.

The one-sentence test did the design work: "OrderService prices the order and emails the confirmation" needed an "and", so it was two classes wearing one vague name. Named honestly, OrderPricer and ConfirmationMailer each carry a whole sentence, and callers can finally use one job without buying the other.

Scope-honest renaming, behavior untouched: GetSubscriber registered strangers and IsActive wrote history, so both names were lies every caller believed. FindOrRegisterSubscriber and RecordCheckAndReportActive tell the truth — and the second name, needing "And", immediately exposes the next refactor. Honest names turn hidden design flaws into visible, countable ones.

exercises.title: Rename a lending desk into the library's language
exercises.smell: Off-domain and dishonest names: the lending desk behaves correctly and the boundary Test Suite starts green, but nothing behind the Target Interface speaks the library's language. The internals are written in borrowed vocabulary — Manager, Process, Data, item, temp, flag — the same domain concept goes by several names in different corners, and several names lie about scope: a Get that creates, a Check that mutates. Rename everything behind the Target Interface into the library's own terms (the glossary in smell-notes.md), Test Suite green after every rename.

exercises.title: Build a front desk that speaks the hotel's language
exercises.smell: The construct temptation is to let implementation vocabulary write the code: dictionaries named dict, loop variables named item, booleans named flag, a helper named Manager — behavior a Test Suite accepts but no hotelier could read. The folder README carries the hotel glossary — guest, room, stay, check-in, check-out, occupied, vacant — and every class, method, and variable you add draws its words from it, each private member's responsibility fitting one sentence without 'and'.

selfCheckQuestions.prompt: Grep your solution for Manager, Helper, Util, Handler, Process, Data, Info, temp, flag, item, and obj. Outside the Target Interface file, is the hit count zero?
selfCheckQuestions.explanation: Words like Manager, Helper, and Data announce that something exists without saying what it is or does. The way out is to ask which noun or verb from the member's one-sentence job is missing from its name. A name that will not come is often the sign that the class holds more than one job.

options.label: No — at least one vague name remains

selfCheckQuestions.prompt: State each class's and each private method's responsibility in one sentence starting with its name. Did any sentence need 'and'?
selfCheckQuestions.explanation: Stating a responsibility in one sentence is a design check wearing a naming check's clothes. A sentence that needs 'and' describes two responsibilities, and the name will keep resisting until they are separated. The missing name is pointing at where to split.

options.label: No — every sentence came out whole

selfCheckQuestions.prompt: For each member you named, read only the name and signature and write down what you expect it to do; then read the body. Count the members that did more, less, or other than the name promised (a Get that creates, an Is that records). Is the count zero?
selfCheckQuestions.explanation: A name should state what a reader would otherwise have to discover by reading the body. When the body does more, less, or other than the name promised, the name misleads once for every hundred times it is read. Side effects the name never mentions, such as a Get that creates a row, are the common form.

options.label: Yes — every name kept its promise
No — at least one body surprised me
